data.name: Old Fashioned
data.description: Whiskey, a little sugar and bitters, stirred and poured over a big cube. The drink every bartender should nail.
steps: Add syrup and bitters to a mixing glass.
Add whiskey and ice. Stir 20–30 seconds.
Strain over a large cube.
Express an orange peel over the top and drop it in.
data.tasteLine: Strong and smooth. Basically whiskey, seasoned.
data.spiritLine: The whiskey is the star. A higher-proof bourbon, or a spicy rye, stands up to the sugar and bitters.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “An Old Fashioned: whiskey, a little sugar and bitters, with an orange peel. Bourbon or rye?”
data.story: One of the oldest cocktails. In the early 1800s a “cocktail” meant spirit, sugar, water and bitters. As drinks got fancier, guests asked for whiskey cocktails made “the old-fashioned way,” and the name stuck.

video.title: How I Make an Old Fashioned · Anders Erickson

data.name: Manhattan
data.description: Rye whiskey and sweet vermouth with bitters, stirred and served up with a cherry. Rich and elegant.
steps: Chill the glass.
Stir everything with ice for about 30 seconds.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.
data.tasteLine: Smooth, rich and a little sweet.
data.spiritLine: Rye’s spice balances the sweet vermouth. That’s why it’s the classic choice.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Manhattan: rye, sweet vermouth and bitters, served up with a cherry.”
data.story: Born in New York in the 1870s or 1880s. A popular story ties it to the Manhattan Club, but nobody knows for sure. It was one of the first cocktails made with vermouth.

video.title: How to Make a Manhattan · Anders Erickson

data.name: Martini
data.description: Gin and dry vermouth, stirred ice-cold and served up with a twist or olives. Simple, so every detail matters.
steps: Chill the glass.
Stir with ice for about 30 seconds, until very cold.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Twist or olives, as the guest asked.
data.spiritLine: A London Dry gin gives the classic crisp, juniper bite.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “Gin or vodka? Olives or a twist?” Always ask both.
data.story: The Martini grew out of sweeter gin-and-vermouth drinks in the late 1800s. Through the 1900s it got drier and drier, and James Bond made “shaken, not stirred” famous.

video.title: How to make a Martini · Anders Erickson

data.name: Negroni
data.description: Gin, Campari and sweet vermouth in equal parts, stirred over ice. Bitter, bold and a classic before dinner.
steps: Stir everything with ice for about 20 seconds.
Strain over a large cube.
Express an orange peel over the top.
data.tasteLine: Bitter first, then sweet and herbal.
data.spiritLine: Campari gives the Negroni its red color and its bitter backbone.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Negroni: gin, Campari and sweet vermouth. Bitter and bold.”
data.story: Legend says Count Camillo Negroni asked for gin instead of soda in his Americano, in Florence around 1919. It became Italy’s classic before-dinner drink.

video.title: The Negroni and the Americano · Anders Erickson

data.name: Boulevardier
data.description: A Negroni made with bourbon or rye instead of gin. Richer and warmer, great for fall and winter.
steps: Stir everything with ice for about 20 seconds.
Strain over a large cube, or up into a coupe.
Express an orange peel over the top.
data.spiritLine: Bourbon makes it rounder and sweeter than a Negroni.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Boulevardier is a Negroni made with whiskey. Richer and warmer.”
data.story: Named after Boulevardier, a magazine for Americans in Paris. It first appeared in a 1927 bar book from Harry’s New York Bar in Paris.

data.name: Sazerac
data.description: Rye, sugar and Peychaud’s bitters in a glass rinsed with absinthe. Served cold with no ice.
steps: Rinse a chilled rocks glass with absinthe and dump the extra.
Stir rye, syrup and bitters with ice.
Strain into the glass, no ice.
Express a lemon peel over the top, then discard it.
data.tasteLine: Aromatic and strong, with a hint of licorice.
data.spiritLine: Rye was the New Orleans standard: spicy and bold.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Sazerac: rye, Peychaud’s bitters and an absinthe rinse. Strong and aromatic.”
data.story: Named after Sazerac cognac, its original base in 1800s New Orleans. Rye took over later. Today it’s the official cocktail of New Orleans.

data.name: Margarita
data.description: Tequila, fresh lime and orange liqueur, shaken and served on the rocks or up, usually with salt.
steps: Salt the rim if the guest wants it (half rim is a nice option).
Shake everything hard with ice.
Strain over fresh ice, or up.
Garnish with a lime wheel.

riffs.name: Tommy’s Margarita
riffs.note: Agave syrup instead of orange liqueur.

data.spiritLine: A 100% agave blanco keeps it bright and peppery.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “Salt, no salt, or half? Rocks or up?”
data.story: Several bartenders in Mexico and the US claimed to invent it in the 1930s and 40s. Nobody knows for sure. Today it’s one of the most popular cocktails in America.

video.title: 5 ways to make a Margarita · Anders Erickson

data.name: Daiquiri
data.description: Rum, fresh lime and sugar, shaken and served up. Not the frozen kind: the classic is three ingredients, perfectly balanced.
steps: Shake hard with ice for 10–12 seconds.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
data.spiritLine: A clean white rum lets the lime shine.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A classic daiquiri: rum, lime and sugar, shaken and served up.”
data.story: Named after a beach near Santiago de Cuba, where Americans mixed rum, lime and sugar around 1900. Hemingway helped make the Havana daiquiri famous.

data.name: Whiskey Sour
data.description: Bourbon, lemon and sugar, often shaken with egg white for a silky foam topped with bitters.
steps: Shake everything without ice first (dry shake) to build the foam.
Add ice and shake again.
Strain over fresh ice.
Add 3 drops of bitters on the foam and a cherry.

riffs.name: New York Sour
riffs.note: A red wine float on top.

data.spiritLine: Bourbon’s vanilla and caramel round out the lemon.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A whiskey sour, made with egg white for a silky foam. With or without egg?”
data.story: Sours go back to sailors mixing spirits with citrus. The Whiskey Sour was in print by the 1860s, and egg white foam is the classic option.

video.title: How to Make the Best Whiskey Sour · Anders Erickson

data.allergyNote: Egg white is raw and optional. Ask every guest, and note it on the ticket.

data.name: Gimlet
data.description: Gin, fresh lime and sugar, shaken and served up. Crisp and bright.
steps: Shake hard with ice.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
data.spiritLine: Gin’s botanicals meet bright lime.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A gimlet: gin and lime, shaken and served up. Crisp and tart.”
data.story: British sailors drank gin with lime cordial; the lime helped prevent scurvy. The Gimlet grew from that habit.

data.name: Cosmopolitan
data.description: Citrus vodka, orange liqueur, lime and a splash of cranberry, shaken and served up. Tart, not sweet.
steps: Shake hard with ice.
Double strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish with an orange peel or lime wheel.
data.tasteLine: Tart, bright and a little fruity.
data.spiritLine: Citrus vodka adds lemon zest under the cranberry.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Cosmo: citrus vodka, orange liqueur, lime and a splash of cranberry. Tart, not sweet.”
data.story: Bartender Toby Cecchini is credited with the modern Cosmo, in New York in 1988. Sex and the City made it famous in the late 1990s.

data.name: Last Word
data.description: Equal parts gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino liqueur and lime. Herbal, tart and a little sweet.
steps: Shake hard with ice.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without a garnish, or with a cherry.

riffs.name: Naked & Famous
riffs.note: Mezcal, Aperol, Yellow Chartreuse and lime.

data.spiritLine: Chartreuse is the soul of the drink: 130 herbs in one bottle.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Last Word: equal parts gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino and lime. It was created right here in Detroit.”
data.story: Created at the Detroit Athletic Club around 1916. It was nearly forgotten until a Seattle bartender brought it back in the early 2000s. A Detroit original.

video.title: How to Make a Last Word · Anders Erickson

data.name: Paper Plane
data.description: Equal parts bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino and lemon. Bittersweet, bright and easy to love.
steps: Shake hard with ice.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish needed.
data.spiritLine: Nonino adds orange and a gentle bittersweet depth.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Paper Plane: bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino and lemon. Bittersweet and bright.”
data.story: Bartender Sam Ross created it in 2007 and named it after the M.I.A. song Paper Planes. It’s a modern classic built on equal parts.

data.name: Penicillin
data.description: Blended Scotch, lemon and honey-ginger syrup, with a float of smoky Islay Scotch on top.
steps: Shake the Scotch, lemon and syrup with ice.
Strain over a large cube.
Gently float the Islay Scotch on top.
Garnish with candied ginger.
data.spiritLine: The smoky Islay float is the drink’s signature.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Penicillin: Scotch with honey, ginger and lemon, and a smoky float on top.”
data.story: Sam Ross created it at Milk & Honey in New York in 2005. It became one of the most copied modern classics.

data.name: Espresso Martini
data.description: Vodka, fresh espresso and coffee liqueur, shaken hard for a thick, creamy foam.
steps: Pull a fresh shot of espresso.
Shake everything very hard with ice to build the foam.
Double strain into a chilled glass.
Float three coffee beans on top.
data.spiritLine: Vodka stays out of the way so the coffee leads.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “An Espresso Martini: vodka, fresh espresso and coffee liqueur, shaken to a creamy foam.”
data.story: London bartender Dick Bradsell created it in the 1980s, when a guest asked for a drink to wake her up.

data.name: Sidecar
data.description: Cognac, orange liqueur and fresh lemon, shaken and served up, often with a sugared rim. The brandy sour every bartender should know.
steps: Sugar half the rim of a chilled coupe, if the guest wants it.
Shake cognac, orange liqueur and lemon hard with ice for 10–12 seconds.
Double strain into the coupe and garnish with an orange twist.
data.tasteLine: Bright and tart, with brandy warmth underneath.

riffs.name: Between the Sheets
riffs.note: Splits the base with light rum.

riffs.name: Brandy Crusta
riffs.note: The older New Orleans cousin, with a full sugar rim.

data.spiritLine: A VS or VSOP cognac gives the drink body and a little oak against the lemon.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Sidecar: cognac, orange liqueur and lemon, shaken and served up. Bright, with a little brandy warmth.”
data.story: Usually traced to Paris or London just after World War I. The popular story says it was named for a customer who rode to the bar in a motorcycle sidecar. Nobody knows for sure.

video.title: How I Make a Sidecar · Anders Erickson

data.name: Pisco Sour
data.description: Pisco, fresh lime, sugar and egg white, shaken into a silky foam and finished with drops of bitters. Peru calls it the national drink, and Chile claims it too.
steps: Shake pisco, lime, syrup and egg white without ice first, to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard again.
Double strain into a chilled coupe and dot the foam with 3 drops of bitters.
data.tasteLine: Tart and bright, with a soft, creamy foam. Tell guests it has raw egg white.

riffs.name: Chilean Pisco Sour
riffs.note: Chilean pisco, often with lemon and no bitters.

data.spiritLine: A grape brandy from Peru and Chile. Its floral fruit is what makes this sour different.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Pisco Sour: pisco, lime and a silky egg-white foam with a few drops of bitters. It does have raw egg white.”
data.story: Usually credited to Victor Morris, an American who ran a bar in Lima, Peru, around the 1920s. Peru and Chile both call the drink their own.
data.allergyNote: Egg white is raw. Ask every guest, and note it on the ticket.

data.name: Paloma
data.description: Tequila, lime and grapefruit soda over ice, with a pinch of salt. Easy and refreshing.
steps: Salt the rim if the guest wants it.
Add tequila, lime and salt to a glass full of ice.
Top with grapefruit soda.
Stir gently and garnish.
data.spiritLine: Blanco tequila keeps it light and bright.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Paloma: tequila and grapefruit soda with lime. Light and refreshing.”
data.story: Its origin is unclear, but it’s a favorite across Mexico, usually made with grapefruit soda.

video.title: The Paloma: Mexico's National Cocktail · Anders Erickson

data.name: Moscow Mule
data.description: Vodka, lime and spicy ginger beer, served in a copper mug over ice.
steps: Fill the mug with ice.
Add vodka and lime.
Top with ginger beer and stir gently.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
data.spiritLine: Vodka lets the spicy ginger beer lead.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Moscow Mule: vodka, lime and ginger beer, in a copper mug.”
data.story: Created in Los Angeles in the 1940s to help sell vodka and ginger beer to Americans. The copper mug was part of the pitch.

data.name: Mojito
data.description: White rum, fresh mint, lime and sugar over crushed ice, topped with soda.
steps: Gently press the mint with syrup and lime. Don’t shred it.
Add rum and crushed ice.
Top with soda and stir up from the bottom.
Clap a mint sprig to wake it up and garnish.

riffs.name: Southside
riffs.note: Gin, mint and lime, served up.

data.spiritLine: A light white rum keeps it fresh and minty.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Mojito: rum, fresh mint and lime with soda. Cool and refreshing.”
data.story: From Cuba, where an older drink of rum, lime, sugar and mint was popular. Havana’s bars made the Mojito world famous.

video.title: Two Ways To Make A Mojito · Anders Erickson

data.name: Aperol Spritz
data.description: Prosecco, Aperol and a splash of soda over ice. Light, bittersweet and made for before dinner.
steps: Fill a wine glass with ice.
Add prosecco first, then Aperol, so it mixes.
Add a splash of soda.
Garnish with an orange slice.
data.spiritLine: Aperol brings the orange glow and gentle bitterness.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “An Aperol Spritz: prosecco and Aperol with soda. Light and bittersweet.”
data.story: Spritzes go back to the 1800s, when Austrian soldiers in the Veneto added a splash of water to local wine. Aperol was created in Padua in 1919.

data.name: French 75
data.description: Gin, lemon and sugar, shaken and topped with Champagne. Bright, bubbly and elegant.
steps: Shake gin, lemon and syrup with ice.
Strain into a flute.
Top slowly with Champagne.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
data.spiritLine: Dry Champagne gives it lift and bubbles.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A French 75: gin, lemon and Champagne. Bright and bubbly.”
data.story: Named after the French 75mm field gun from World War I, because the drink packs a punch.

video.title: How to make a French 75 · Anders Erickson

data.name: Lemon Drop
data.description: Vodka, fresh lemon and orange liqueur, shaken and served up in a sugar-rimmed glass. Sweet, tart and easy.
steps: Rim a chilled glass with sugar.
Shake vodka, lemon, orange liqueur and syrup hard with ice.
Strain into the glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
data.tasteLine: Sweet and tart, like a lemon candy.

riffs.name: Raspberry Lemon Drop
riffs.note: Add raspberry liqueur or muddled raspberries.

riffs.name: Lemon Drop Shot
riffs.note: Same build, served as a shot with a sugared lemon wedge.

data.spiritLine: A clean vodka lets the lemon lead.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Lemon Drop: vodka, lemon and orange liqueur, shaken and served in a sugar-rimmed glass. Sweet and tart.”
data.story: Usually credited to Henry Africa’s, a San Francisco bar, in the 1970s. Bar lead to check the history.
